q: Thirty-six months on the lees, a second fermentation in the bottle, and fruit harvested and pressed in one named municipality. Which tier of Sekt Austria is that?
exp: Grosse Reserve tops the pyramid at thirty-six months on the lees and is the only tier that requires the grapes to be harvested and pressed inside a single Gemeinde, with a named Ried permitted on top of that. Reserve sits below it at eighteen months and takes the federal state as its origin, though it too may name a municipality; both must be hand-harvested and bottle-fermented.

q: Entry-level Sekt Austria may be produced in tank rather than in bottle, but it still owes a minimum time on its lees. How long?
exp: The base tier draws its fruit from a single federal state and permits any method suited to sparkling wine: six months on the lees if the wine ferments in tank, nine if it ferments in the bottle. The eighteen and thirty-six month figures belong to Reserve and Grosse Reserve, both of which must ferment in the bottle they are sold in.

q: An Austrian label and a German label both read Kabinett, yet the word does not sit on the same rung in the two systems. Where does Austria place it?
opts: As a category of Qualitatswein, not a Pradikat
As the lowest Pradikat, exactly as Germany does
As a term reserved for sparkling wine
exp: Austrian Kabinett is unchaptalised Qualitatswein with a ceiling on both alcohol and residual sugar, and the Pradikat ladder starts above it at Spatlese. The ladders differ at the top as well: Austria recognises Ausbruch and Strohwein, which German law does not.

q: Ripeness at harvest is read in Austria on a scale named after a monastery north of Vienna. Which scale?
exp: One degree KMW is one gram of sugar in a hundred grams of must, so the figure runs at roughly a fifth of the German Oechsle reading for the same juice. Klosterneuburg also houses a school of viticulture founded in 1860, where Zweigelt was bred.

q: One short word must stand in front of a single-vineyard name on an Austrian label, so a site cannot be mistaken for a village. Which word?
exp: Ried is Austrian dialect for a delimited parcel of vineyard, and the wine law requires it to precede the name: Ried Heiligenstein, Ried Achleiten. Ort means place and belongs to the village tier, while Lage is not the required prefix; Austrian law has since 2023 provided for Erste Lage and Grosse Lage as classifications that sit on top of a Riedenwein rather than replacing the word Ried.

q: Brewers at Burton-on-Trent drew on a well water heavy in calcium sulphate, and the pale ales made there gained a notably dry, sharpened bitterness. What is the practice of dosing water elsewhere to imitate that called?
exp: Sulphate accentuates hop bitterness and dryness, while carbonate-rich water suits dark roasted grain instead, which is part of why Dublin became a stout town and Burton a pale ale one. Modern brewers build whatever profile they want by adding salts to stripped water.

q: Alongside a useful load of enzymes, one grain carries a tough outer husk that settles into a natural filter bed when the sweet liquid is drawn off. Which grain is the brewer's default?
exp: Wheat and rye are huskless and turn a mash gluey and slow to run, so they are used as part of a grist rather than alone. Barley's husk and its high enzyme content are why it, and not any other cereal, became the base of beer.

q: Long before refrigeration, beers sent on lengthy sea voyages were loaded with extra quantities of one ingredient whose resins hold spoilage bacteria back. Which ingredient?
exp: Hop alpha acids are mildly antibacterial as well as bitter, so hopping doubled as preservation in an age with no other option. That is the practical root of the heavily hopped export styles, of which India Pale Ale is the famous survivor.

q: Fermentable sugar disappears from the wort and alcohol, carbon dioxide and a crowd of aroma compounds appear in its place. Which of the four raw materials did that work?
exp: Malt supplies the sugar and hops the bitterness, but only yeast converts the one into the other. Strain choice also sets much of the finished flavour, which is why an identical wort can end up as two beers that taste nothing alike.

q: Bavaria's purity law of 1516 listed only three permitted ingredients, and the omission was ignorance rather than intent. Which ingredient is missing from that list?
exp: Yeast had not been identified, and brewers pitched the dregs of a previous batch without knowing what was in them. Later restatements of the Reinheitsgebot added it once Pasteur and Hansen had explained what was actually doing the work.

q: Grain is steeped in water, allowed to sprout, then dried to halt the sprouting before the growing shoot eats the starch. What is that whole sequence called?
exp: The maltster does this work, usually in a business separate from the brewery. Arresting germination at the right moment is the skill: too early and the enzymes are weak, too late and the seed has spent the starch the brewer came for.

q: Persuading barley to sprout is laborious and costs the maltster some of the starch outright. What does germination create that makes it worth doing?
opts: Enzymes able to cut starch into fermentable sugar
exp: Amylase enzymes develop as the seed prepares to feed its own shoot, and the brewer hijacks them in the mash tun. Raw unmalted grain holds plenty of starch but has no means of releasing it.

q: Two malts are made from the same barley: one is dried gently and stays pale straw, the other is taken to fierce heat and comes out almost black. Which step accounts for the difference?
opts: The moisture content of the grain at harvest
exp: Kilning temperature and duration drive browning reactions, so colour and flavour climb together from bready through toffee to coffee. Hard roasting also destroys the enzymes, which is why dark malts appear in small proportions beside a pale base.

q: The dry coffee and bitter-chocolate bite of an Irish stout, and its near-black colour, come from one part of the grist. Which?
opts: A high dose of Munich malt
A large proportion of crystal malt
exp: Roasted barley is taken so far in the kiln that it contributes astringency and roast rather than sugar, while crystal and Munich malts give caramel and bread rather than coffee and flaked maize gives almost no flavour at all. Chocolate and black malts do comparable work in porter, and it is that roast character that separates the family from brown ales.

q: Milled malt meets hot water in the first vessel of the brewhouse and rests there while the enzymes work. What is the sweet liquid run off afterwards called?
exp: Must is the grape equivalent and belongs to winemaking. Trub is the protein and hop sludge that drops out after the boil, and krausen is the foam head that sits on an actively fermenting beer.

q: Once the sweet liquid has been drawn off, the spent grain bed still holds recoverable sugar, so hot water is trickled through it. What is that rinse called?
exp: Sparge water is kept hot enough for the liquid to run freely but not so hot that it strips harsh tannin out of the husks. Rinse too far and the last runnings turn thin and astringent.
